title: Mineral Rights — Operator Companion Workbook
subtitle: 6 Printable Operator Worksheets for Mineral and NPRI Underwriting, Pooling-Docket Research, Royalty Reconciliation, Capital Discipline, and Institutional Exits

worksheets.title: Opportunity Underwriting and Counterparty Qualification
worksheets.purpose: Turn a mineral acquisition lead into a documented investment decision before committing capital. Establish the exact property interest, ownership chain, production exposure, development catalyst, seller authority, and realistic institutional buyer universe while separating recorded facts from speculative drilling expectations.
instructions: Select one county, producing formation, and acquisition strategy before reviewing offers. Assemble the recorded instruments, lease schedule, production history, public docket entries, and ownership evidence into one dated packet so underwriting assumptions remain traceable to source documents.

Calculate net mineral acres separately from royalty ownership. Read every reservation and granting clause before applying a lease royalty fraction, and obtain a title professional's written interpretation whenever fixed, floating, term, or depth-limited interests create competing decimal outcomes.

Treat pooling applications, permits, and operator presentations as research inputs rather than completed development. Record hearing dates, protests, final orders, elections, and expiration conditions, then price a delayed-development case alongside the proposed near-term drilling case.

Verify seller identity and signing authority through independently obtained records and a trusted callback. Compare the payment recipient with the deed grantor and estate or entity documents before allowing an executed purchase agreement to enter closing.

Identify potential institutional buyers using completed transactions and their stated acquisition criteria. Document acreage thresholds, title expectations, data requirements, and concentration limits without treating an indicative conversation as a binding bid or a guaranteed resale channel.

fields.name: County, formation, and acquisition thesis
fields.prompt: Define the geographic boundary, target formation, interest type, investment duration, and observable reason the property fits your strategy. State what evidence would invalidate the thesis before contacting additional owners.
fields.example: Target producing oil and gas minerals in one defined Reeves County, Texas, acquisition area, with a thirty-six-month holding case. Require recorded ownership and twelve monthly check details. Reject purchases supported only by neighboring permits when the subject tract has no documented development or producing allocation.

fields.name: Interest classification and conveyance language
fields.prompt: Quote the operative grant and reservation language, then classify mineral, executive, royalty, and depth rights separately. Explain whether an NPRI fraction is fixed or floating and identify unresolved construction questions.
fields.example: Instrument A conveys an undivided one-fourth mineral interest in 160 gross acres without a listed depth limitation. Instrument B reserves one-fourth of the royalty, requiring separate floating-NPRI analysis. Do not label both instruments forty royalty acres or combine their burdens without tracing which estate each instrument affects.

fields.name: Net mineral acres and unit decimal
fields.prompt: Show gross acres, mineral ownership, lease royalty, unit acreage, and the allocation method actually authorized by the governing documents. Identify burdens and participation adjustments before accepting a revenue decimal.
fields.example: For an unburdened illustrative tract, 160 gross acres times 25% ownership equals 40 NMA. With a 20% lease royalty and valid acreage allocation across 1,280 acres, the decimal is 40 divided by 1,280 times 0.20, or 0.00625. Confirm this allocation rather than importing it into every horizontal unit.

fields.name: Fixed and floating NPRI comparison
fields.prompt: Model competing royalty interpretations using the actual tract allocation and lease fraction. Preserve the instrument language alongside each calculation, and explain why an NPRI must not automatically be multiplied by royalty twice.
fields.example: Across a fully represented 160-acre tract in a 1,280-acre unit, a fixed 1/64 royalty yields 0.015625 times 160/1,280 equals 0.001953125. A floating one-fourth of a 20% royalty yields 0.00625 instead. These alternative examples assume no additional ownership fraction, burdens, or allocation adjustments.

fields.name: Recorded chain and severance investigation
fields.prompt: List the deed chain, mineral severances, probate links, liens, reservations, and depth restrictions that establish saleable ownership. Assign a responsible reviewer and a specific corrective document for every material break.
fields.example: The seller's 2018 deed references a 1974 mineral reservation and a 2009 estate distribution. The landman retrieves both instruments and the probate order; the title attorney resolves whether the reserved interest remains outstanding. A missing heir conveyance blocks funding until an acceptable recorded curative instrument establishes the seller's interest.

fields.name: Production, decline, and operator concentration
fields.prompt: Summarize monthly production, realized pricing, downtime, well age, decline assumptions, and operator exposure. Distinguish historical reported volumes from forecast volumes, and identify whether public data represent wells, leases, or allocated units.
fields.example: Twelve purchaser statements support $18,750 of annual gross royalty on Tract A before specified deductions. The downside case applies a 20% volume decline and 25% price reduction, producing $11,250 before deductions. One operator controls all current cash flow, so the file separately models ninety days of payment interruption.

fields.name: Pooling-docket catalyst and jurisdiction
fields.prompt: Identify the agency, proceeding type, tract coverage, public event dates, and legal effect of each docket development. Separate a filed application from an effective order and an effective order from production.
fields.example: For an illustrative Oklahoma prospect, track the pooling application under 52 O.S. § 87.1, service evidence, hearing, final order, and owner election deadline. A scheduled hearing does not establish completed pooling or drilling. Keep this Oklahoma workflow separate from Texas Mineral Interest Pooling Act analysis under Natural Resources Code Chapter 102.

fields.name: Seller identity and authority
fields.prompt: Record the grantor's verified identity, ownership capacity, authorized signer, independent contact source, and payment instructions. Identify estate, trust, entity, or marital documents that must be reviewed before execution and disbursement.
fields.example: A Texas limited liability company owns the minerals, while an individual negotiates the sale. Obtain its formation record, governing authority, and transaction authorization. Confirm the signer through an independently sourced telephone number, then require the escrow recipient to match documented ownership rather than a newly emailed personal bank account.

fields.name: Institutional buyer qualification and exit fit
fields.prompt: Name the intended buyer category, minimum package size, producing exposure, acceptable jurisdictions, title standards, and required data format. Record the difference between a qualified buyer conversation and an executable purchase offer.
fields.example: The target buyer acquires producing Permian mineral packages with at least $100,000 annual documented royalty receipts. Our $18,750 tract is an aggregation component, not a standalone institutional package. The buyer requests tract polygons, recorded deeds, payor decimals, and twenty-four months of statements before providing a priced indication.

fields.name: Investment decision and kill criteria
fields.prompt: State the maximum purchase price, approved assumptions, remaining conditions, responsible decision maker, and explicit rejection triggers. Explain which uncertainty can be priced and which uncertainty prevents an acquisition entirely.
fields.example: Authorize an indicative price ceiling of $120,000 for Tract A only after the forty NMA and 0.00625 decimal are established. Reject unresolved competing ownership or unverifiable seller authority. A drilling delay may justify a lower price; a missing ownership link cannot be solved merely by assuming a higher future commodity price.

worksheets.completion_gate: Advance only when the acquisition lead, title reviewer, and capital owner have signed the source-linked ownership calculation, downside valuation, counterparty verification, and written rejection criteria.

worksheets.title: Unit Economics, Defect Reserve, and Working-Capital Float
worksheets.purpose: Build an acquisition and portfolio model that preserves the distinction between mineral purchase capital, royalty receipts, realized trading gains, operating costs, and owner profit. Quantify title-curative exposure, payment delays, commodity sensitivity, and liquidity without inflating revenue through returned investment basis.
instructions: Lock the three canonical portfolio scenarios before entering tract assumptions. Use the stated revenue and owner-profit figures exactly, label supporting allocations as illustrative, and never represent one acquisition's cash yield as the entire portfolio's net margin.

Maintain separate schedules for acquisition basis, realized gain, recurring royalties, overhead, direct transaction costs, and cash restrictions. Reconcile bank movement to those schedules rather than classifying every incoming wire as recognized operator revenue or spendable profit.

Build the royalty forecast from verified ownership decimals and an explicit unit revenue assumption. Show production decline, commodity price, deductions, and downtime separately so a reviewer can identify the exact input responsible for each valuation change.

Size the title-defect reserve from identified curative tasks and credible downside costs. Treat a cash designation as a liquidity decision rather than an automatic expense, and release reserved funds only after documented resolution or a revised written exposure assessment.

Stress payment suspension and delayed resale together, then confirm the business can fund overhead without forced asset sales. State distribution limits and capital-call assumptions explicitly; an attractive paper gain does not pay a near-term legal invoice.

fields.name: Canonical portfolio scenario lock
fields.prompt: Enter annual gross revenue, net margin, owner net profit, and team size for all three canonical scenarios. Calculate implied total costs and preserve these figures when adding detailed operating assumptions.
fields.example: Conservative: $30,000 revenue, 20% margin, $6,000 profit, $24,000 costs, 1 FT plus 3 C. Base: $215,000, 32.5%, $69,875, $145,125 costs, 1 FT plus 3 C. Scaled: $400,000, 45%, $180,000, $220,000 costs, 2 FT plus 4 C, totaling six people.

fields.name: Recognized revenue and returned basis bridge
fields.prompt: Bridge royalty receipts and realized rights-trading gains to total recognized operator revenue. Show gross disposal proceeds and returned basis separately, and identify whether transaction costs are expensed or included in basis.
fields.example: Illustrative Base revenue combines $175,000 royalty receipts and $40,000 realized gain. A $160,000 Tract B sale returns $120,000 recorded basis and creates that $40,000 gain. Total incoming receipts are $335,000, but recognized operator revenue remains $215,000. Selling costs sit within the stated expense bridge, not inside the gain again.

fields.name: Purchase basis and royalty cash yield
fields.prompt: Record the acquisition's capitalized basis and its forecast royalty receipts before and after specified deductions. Distinguish unlevered cash yield from owner net margin, and disclose any acquisition costs excluded from the illustrative calculation.
fields.example: Tract A has an illustrative $120,000 recorded basis. Annual unit sales of $3,000,000 times 0.00625 produce $18,750 before deductions, a 15.625% gross cash yield. Assumed annual deductions of $1,650 reduce receipts to $17,100 and the cash yield to 14.25%, before portfolio overhead and income taxes.

fields.name: Commodity and depletion stress calculation
fields.prompt: Recalculate the acquisition under separate price, volume, and payment-interruption stresses. State which costs remain fixed, which deductions move with sales, and whether the analysis includes new wells or only existing production.
fields.example: Apply 20% lower production and 25% lower realized price to the $18,750 gross royalty forecast: $18,750 times 0.80 times 0.75 equals $11,250. For a simple downside test, hold $1,650 deductions constant, leaving $9,600 before overhead. No future wells or sale appreciation rescue this existing-production calculation.

fields.name: Title scrub and defect reserve
fields.prompt: Itemize title-review, curative, recording, and disputed-payment exposures with expected timing and responsible owners. Separate a designated cash reserve from booked expense and explain what evidence permits each reserve release.
fields.example: Designate $15,000 cash for a $6,000 heirship curative, $4,000 specialist title review, $2,000 recording and document retrieval allowance, and $3,000 contingency. This designation is not itself an expense. The accountant classifies actual invoices once incurred; the acquisition lead releases unused cash only after the title reviewer accepts the recorded cure.

fields.name: Working-capital float and receipt suspension
fields.prompt: Calculate the cash needed for overhead, expected receipt delays, and curative work before distributions. Identify double counting between lost receipts and funded overhead, and define the minimum unrestricted cash balance required throughout the stress period.
fields.example: At $6,000 monthly cash overhead, six months require $36,000. Add the separately designated $15,000 curative reserve for a $51,000 liquidity target. A ninety-day suspension of $1,425 monthly Tract A receipts delays $4,275; do not add that amount again when the six-month model already assumes zero receipts.

fields.name: Base expense and profit reconciliation
fields.prompt: Allocate the Base scenario's implied annual costs across overhead, transaction work, specialist support, and administration. Make the arithmetic reconcile exactly and explain which line items are recurring versus acquisition-dependent costs.
fields.example: Base costs comprise $72,000 recurring overhead, $31,000 specialist title and land support, $18,000 deal diligence and sale execution, $12,125 accounting and administration, and $12,000 other operating expense. Total costs equal $145,125; subtracting them from $215,000 revenue produces $69,875 owner net profit, exactly 32.5%.

fields.name: Startup capital and cash allocation
fields.prompt: Choose a startup capitalization within the canonical range and allocate it between purchases, liquidity, curative exposure, and undeployed capital. Preserve the distinction between cash spent on assets and current-period operating expense.
fields.example: An illustrative $400,000 capitalization sits within the $15,000–$75,000 range. Allocate $120,000 each to Tracts A and B, $36,000 overhead float, $15,000 curative cash, and $109,000 uncommitted capital. These allocations total $400,000; they do not create $240,000 of immediate operating expense simply because two mineral purchases close.

fields.name: Scaled workload and cost capacity
fields.prompt: Test whether the Scaled scenario's staffing and cost envelope can support the portfolio's actual statement volume, title workload, and acquisitions. Separate recurring monthly overhead from annual variable transaction and specialist costs.
fields.example: Scaled revenue of $400,000 less $220,000 total costs leaves $180,000 owner net profit. Illustratively, recurring overhead is $10,000 monthly, with $100,000 annual variable costs beyond it. Two full-time operators and four contractors cover acquisition, reconciliation, land, title, accounting, and data work without exceeding six people.

fields.name: Capital release and distribution rule
fields.prompt: Specify when cash may leave the business and which balances remain restricted by operating policy. Reconcile sale proceeds, expenses, reserve requirements, and proposed distributions without treating returned basis as earned operating profit.
fields.example: After Tract B sells for $160,000, tag $120,000 as returned investment basis and $40,000 as realized gain before separately recorded expenses. Distributions require the next six months of overhead plus unresolved curative exposure to remain funded. Reinvestment of returned basis is a capital decision, not a profit margin improvement.

worksheets.completion_gate: Advance only when all three canonical scenarios reconcile exactly, the Base cash-to-revenue bridge excludes returned basis, and the stressed cash schedule funds overhead and identified defects without relying on an uncontracted sale.

worksheets.title: Execution, Ownership Ledger, and Technical Pre-Flight
worksheets.purpose: Convert an approved acquisition into recorded ownership, correct payor setup, and auditable receipts. Establish document controls, parcel identifiers, closing instructions, decimal verification, transaction coding, and exception handling so title defects and payment errors cannot disappear inside a successful-looking dashboard.
instructions: Assign immutable identifiers before importing documents or sending purchase agreements. Link the property, instrument, owner, lease, well, unit, and payor through explicit relationships rather than assuming an operator's property number uniquely identifies the mineral estate.

Prepare a closing checklist that distinguishes executed documents, verified authority, cleared conditions, recorded instruments, and disbursed funds. A signed deed alone does not prove recording, and a bank debit does not prove the correct recipient received payment.

Recalculate ownership decimals from source instruments before accepting division-order values. Compare the payor's allocation method with lease and unit documents, then route any unexplained difference to a named reviewer rather than silently forcing the ledger to match.

Reconcile each statement line to production month, product, price, volume, taxes, deductions, and cash settlement. Preserve adjustments as separate records so retroactive corrections remain visible and do not overwrite the original accounting or supporting evidence.

Complete a technical pre-flight with duplicate files, revised statements, suspended payments, and mismatched decimals before importing a live portfolio. Define rollback procedures and retain original source files so an incorrect parser release can be reversed cleanly.

fields.name: Property master and relationship keys
fields.prompt: Define stable identifiers for tracts, interests, leases, wells, units, and payors. Record how multiple wells relate to one tract and how changed operator identifiers are preserved without creating duplicate assets.
fields.example: Use TRACT-023-001 for Tract A and INTEREST-023-001 for its purchased mineral estate. Store county recording references separately from operator property codes. Two wells may share the same unit but retain distinct well identifiers. An operator transfer creates a dated payor relationship, not a second copy of the purchased forty NMA.

fields.name: Document manifest and evidence versions
fields.prompt: List every required source document with its origin, retrieval date, version, and integrity fingerprint. Explain how a revised instrument interpretation changes derived calculations without deleting the earlier evidence or reviewer comments.
fields.example: The manifest includes the recorded vesting deed, lease, amendments, unit instrument, title memorandum, purchase agreement, and twelve statements. Python hashlib computes SHA-256 fingerprints for stored files. A corrected title memorandum receives version two; version one remains retained and marked superseded, with the resulting decimal change linked to both versions.

fields.name: Purchase agreement and closing sequence
fields.prompt: Set the order of diligence completion, execution, funding, recording, and evidence delivery. Name the person responsible for each step and specify the evidence needed before the escrow agent releases purchase funds.
fields.example: The agreement identifies the exact conveyed interest, a $120,000 purchase price, the effective date, permitted burdens, and title remedies. Escrow receives funds only after authority review. Release follows the agreed recording protocol and verified instructions; the closing file retains the stamped instrument, disbursement statement, and independent wire confirmation.

fields.name: Wire verification and exception response
fields.prompt: Document the trusted callback process, approved recipient, dual verification responsibility, and response to changed bank instructions. State which evidence stops disbursement and how an attempted substitution is preserved for investigation.
fields.example: The acquisition lead calls the escrow officer using a previously verified number, while the operations reviewer compares account details against the signed closing instructions. An email changes the recipient two hours before funding; disbursement stops immediately. Retain the message and headers, contact escrow independently, and resume only after the discrepancy is resolved.

fields.name: Division order and payor onboarding
fields.prompt: Identify required payor forms, ownership evidence, tax documentation, effective dates, and decimal review steps. Explain how division-order language is checked against the lease rather than accepted as a replacement for underlying rights.
fields.example: Submit the recorded deed, requested ownership documentation, secure tax form, and verified contact information. Compare the offered 0.00500 decimal with the supported 0.00625 calculation before signing. For Texas production, the reviewer checks relevant division-order requirements under Natural Resources Code § 91.402 and requests correction with the supporting tract calculation attached.

fields.name: Statement normalization and receipt ledger
fields.prompt: Specify the normalized statement columns and bank-matching rules. Preserve production month separately from payment date and identify how taxes, transportation, processing, adjustments, and suspense releases appear in the accounting trail.
fields.example: A monthly line shows $250,000 unit sales times 0.00625 equals $1,562.50 gross royalty. Separately record $93.75 taxes and $43.75 other stated deductions, leaving $1,425 cash. The ledger stores production month, payment date, statement reference, bank transaction, and deduction descriptions so the $137.50 reduction remains inspectable.

fields.name: Decimal variance and deduction dispute
fields.prompt: Set tolerances for ownership and payment differences and define the evidence required to open a payor inquiry. Distinguish a mathematical discrepancy from a disputed contractual deduction and assign each issue a resolution deadline.
fields.example: At $250,000 unit sales, a 0.00500 decimal produces $1,250 rather than the expected $1,562.50 gross royalty, a $312.50 difference. Open a decimal inquiry with the recorded deed and allocation calculation. Separately challenge the $43.75 charge only after reviewing the lease's valuation and deduction provisions; the two issues require different evidence.

fields.name: Asset basis and disposition ledger
fields.prompt: Define the asset-level records supporting acquisition basis, later adjustments, partial disposals, and realized gains. Explain how the operating ledger reconciles to tax-basis schedules without assuming both schedules always carry identical balances.
fields.example: Tract B's operating schedule records $120,000 basis and $160,000 sale proceeds, producing $40,000 realized gain before separately expensed sale costs. The accountant maintains any depletion-related tax adjustments in a linked schedule. A partial sale requires a documented basis allocation before posting gain; the full original basis cannot be deducted on every partial disposition.

fields.name: Parser tests and duplicate prevention
fields.prompt: Describe test fixtures for statement ingestion, revised payments, ownership changes, and malformed numbers. Define idempotency keys and expected results so repeated imports cannot multiply royalty revenue or erase historical adjustments.
fields.example: Load the same statement twice and require one posted receipt. Use file fingerprints plus payor, owner account, statement identifier, and line identity for matching. A revised statement becomes a linked correction. A parenthesized $125.00 adjustment posts as negative $125.00, while an unreadable amount enters manual review instead of silently becoming zero.

fields.name: Month-end certification and recovery plan
fields.prompt: State the close checklist, reviewer responsibilities, unresolved exception presentation, and restoration procedure. Identify the evidence proving recorded receipts match bank activity and that ownership changes have reached each relevant payor.
fields.example: By business day ten, the bookkeeper ties receipts to bank deposits and the operations lead reviews all decimal changes and suspended balances. Unresolved items remain visible with owners and dates. Before updating the parser, retain a read-only ledger export and database backup; restore and replay the test set if reconciliation totals change unexpectedly.

worksheets.completion_gate: Advance only when closing evidence is complete, recorded ownership and payor decimals reconcile, duplicate-import tests pass, and the first available receipt or documented suspense entry matches the asset-level ledger.

worksheets.title: Statutory, Contract, Tax, and Outreach Audit
worksheets.purpose: Translate jurisdiction-specific mineral, leasing, pooling, tax, brokerage, securities, and outreach requirements into documented operating tasks. Identify the exact activity being performed, the controlling authority, the required specialist review, and the evidence necessary before signing instruments, soliciting owners, or accepting investor capital.
instructions: Map every property and business activity to its jurisdiction before choosing forms or outreach methods. Separate direct ownership purchases from representing another party, and distinguish private mineral interests from federal, state, or tribal leases with additional requirements.

Have the title reviewer resolve severances, reservations, probate authority, marital interests, and recordation requirements using the actual chain. Do not replace instrument analysis with a county tax listing, a seller spreadsheet, or a payor's existing ownership decimal.

Convert lease and purchase provisions into measurable obligations covering effective dates, deductions, pooling authority, warranties, curative periods, and payment remedies. Record the controlling clause beside each operational action instead of relying on a generic contract summary.

Review tax classification, licensing exposure, and capital solicitation before launching the relevant activity. Document the specific statutory pathway and supporting records; the fact that mineral assets are tangible property does not resolve every pooled-investment securities question.

Approve outreach scripts by channel and retain suppression records, source permissions, and complaint handling instructions. Stop a campaign when ownership identity, recipient restrictions, or message accuracy cannot be verified, while continuing permitted research and non-contact diligence work.

fields.name: Jurisdiction and property-regime map
fields.prompt: Identify the property location, ownership regime, regulator, recording office, and additional approvals that attach to the specific estate. Explain which familiar private-land workflow cannot be reused without modification.
fields.example: The pilot acquires privately owned Texas minerals and records conveyances with the appropriate county clerk. A later prospect involving a federal oil and gas lease requires separate review of 43 CFR Part 3100 and applicable assignment rules. Exclude that prospect from the private-mineral template until the relevant transfer requirements are mapped.

fields.name: Conveyance, recording, and ownership authority
fields.prompt: List the instrument execution and recording requirements applicable to the transaction, including authority and property description review. Identify the statute and the documented title condition that must be resolved before funding.
fields.example: For a Texas conveyance, review Property Code §§ 5.021, 12.001, and 13.001 for relevant conveyance, recording, and notice requirements. The deed must accurately identify the transferred estate and authorized grantor. A probate representative's signature is accepted only after reviewing the appointment and scope of authority supporting this particular sale.

fields.name: Lease terms and payment obligations
fields.prompt: Extract royalty valuation, deductions, pooling, retained-acreage, depth, cessation, and payment provisions from the governing lease. Link each provision to a calculation or monitoring task and identify statutory payment exceptions requiring further review.
fields.example: The lease states a one-fifth royalty and contains a negotiated transportation provision that requires clause-specific interpretation. Review Texas Natural Resources Code §§ 91.402–91.403 for applicable payment timing, withholding grounds, and interest. A suspended payment triggers a written reason request; it does not automatically establish that statutory interest is owed.

fields.name: Pooling authority and owner election calendar
fields.prompt: Specify whether pooling arises from contract, voluntary agreement, or a statutory proceeding. Record notice, hearing, election, and payment deadlines from the actual documents rather than applying another state's default timeline.
fields.example: An Oklahoma pooling order under 52 O.S. § 87.1 requires the team to extract the exact election and payment terms from the entered order. For Texas, evaluate contractual pooling authority and any proposed proceeding under Natural Resources Code Chapter 102 separately. Neither workflow treats a filed application as an effective conveyance or a completed well.

fields.name: Purchase protections and defect remedies
fields.prompt: Draft the operational meaning of the title standard, defect threshold, curative period, purchase-price adjustment, closing condition, and remedy. Ensure the agreement allocates risk explicitly rather than relying on an undocumented promise to fix title later.
fields.example: The purchase agreement schedules forty NMA, specifies the conveyed depths, and permits a price adjustment for verified acreage shortfalls under its stated formula. A material unresolved ownership defect permits termination before funding. An escrow holdback secures only defined curative obligations; it does not transform disputed ownership into established title.

fields.name: Activity-based licensing assessment
fields.prompt: Describe whether the business purchases for its own account, negotiates for others, receives transaction compensation, or performs specialist services. Obtain a jurisdiction-specific assessment of licensing requirements and document the activities actually authorized.
fields.example: The initial business buys minerals for its own portfolio and pays a land contractor for documented research. Before accepting a success fee to negotiate another owner's sale, obtain a Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1101 analysis covering the interest, activity, and any applicable exclusion. Do not assume the contractor's job title settles the licensing question.

fields.name: Royalty tax and depletion workpaper
fields.prompt: Assign responsibility for royalty reporting, production taxes, property taxes, depletion analysis, basis adjustments, and disposition reporting. Distinguish operating scorecard profit from the separate tax calculations that depend on owner and property circumstances.
fields.example: The accountant reviews 26 U.S.C. §§ 611, 612, 613, and 613A when evaluating depletion eligibility and limitations. Texas production-tax review considers Tax Code Chapters 201 and 202. Maintain supporting statements and tax-basis adjustments separately; a depletion deduction does not increase the canonical Base operating profit above $69,875.

fields.name: Pooled capital and securities pathway
fields.prompt: Describe who contributes capital, who manages the assets, how returns are presented, and whether interests are offered publicly. Require a documented securities analysis before soliciting passive investors or accepting pooled investment subscriptions.
fields.example: Three passive investors propose funding an operator-managed mineral entity. Review Securities Act § 2(a)(1), 15 U.S.C. § 77b(a)(1), including investment-contract and fractional mineral-interest issues. If using Regulation D, select and satisfy the applicable 17 CFR § 230.506 pathway, required filings, state notices, and relevant intermediary or adviser analysis before solicitation.

fields.name: Owner outreach and suppression controls
fields.prompt: Define permitted outreach channels, contact data sources, message representations, opt-out handling, and retention rules. Map telephone, text, and commercial email requirements to the specific campaign rather than treating all channels alike.
fields.example: Start with accurate direct mail identifying the purchasing entity and property interest. Before phone or text outreach, assess 47 U.S.C. § 227, 47 CFR § 64.1200, and applicable state restrictions. Commercial email review uses 15 U.S.C. § 7704. Suppress opted-out recipients promptly and never imply that a county office endorsed the offer.

fields.name: Liens, secured interests, and release evidence
fields.prompt: Identify recorded mortgages, judgments, assignment restrictions, and financing claims that may affect the acquired estate or proceeds. Explain which searches and releases are required and why one database cannot establish clear title.
fields.example: The title reviewer searches the real-property records and evaluates relevant UCC filings. UCC § 9-109(d)(11) addresses the real-property exclusion with exceptions, while § 9-502(b) addresses specified real-property-related filings. A seller's lender claims as-extracted collateral; obtain a transaction-specific release analysis rather than assuming a standard UCC termination alone clears the mineral conveyance.

worksheets.completion_gate: Advance only when every applicable statutory and contract task has an owner, source citation, and retained evidence; unresolved title authority, licensing scope, investor solicitation, or restricted outreach prevents the affected activity from proceeding.

worksheets.title: Automation, Owner Outreach, and Risk Fallback Tracker
worksheets.purpose: Design a small-team operating system that automates royalty reconciliation and production monitoring while preserving human judgment for title, valuation, and owner communications. Build a repeatable acquisition pipeline with explicit data provenance, review queues, failure alerts, and manual recovery procedures.
instructions: Start with a narrow data flow connecting authorized source documents to a normalized ledger and exception queue. Automate deterministic checks first, retain original evidence, and keep ownership interpretation and purchase-price decisions assigned to named human reviewers.

Establish production-monitoring thresholds using reporting frequency and known data delays. Differentiate missing reports, revised volumes, well downtime, and actual depletion before sending alerts or changing valuations, particularly where public reporting aggregates several wells.

Build outreach from verified ownership records and a single suppression list shared across the team. Measure qualified conversations and complete underwriting packets rather than rewarding raw message volume, repeated contacts, or unverified owner matches.

Use public pooling and permit information to prioritize research, not to represent certain development. Require source links and dated status transitions, then record why each catalyst changed the acquisition queue without automatically raising the offer.

Define fallback procedures before deploying each automation. A source outage, parser error, disputed decimal, or exposed credential must have an owner, recovery target, manual operating method, and documented condition for returning to routine processing.

fields.name: Authorized source inventory and cadence
fields.prompt: List each production, title, docket, and payment source with access method, refresh frequency, permitted use, and responsible owner. Separate authoritative records from useful secondary indexes that require confirmation before decisions.
fields.example: Use Texas Railroad Commission public production records for monitoring, county clerk instruments for recorded conveyances, and operator statements for payor-specific receipts. Review Oklahoma Corporation Commission docket updates for designated prospects. Refresh production monthly and active dockets twice weekly, using permitted downloads and retaining source dates instead of bypassing access restrictions.

fields.name: Normalization pipeline and validation rules
fields.prompt: Describe ingestion, parsing, validation, storage, review, and export stages. Define required fields and numerical checks that reject unreliable records without discarding the original source or inventing missing ownership and payment values.
fields.example: A Python stdlib workflow uses csv for exports, decimal for money, sqlite3 for records, and hashlib for file identity. It checks that gross royalty minus listed deductions equals payment within one cent. Missing production month or unreadable decimal sends the record to review with its original attachment and failure reason preserved.

fields.name: Royalty reconciliation automation
fields.prompt: Define automated comparisons between expected ownership, reported sales, deductions, and bank receipts. State numerical alert thresholds and identify which discrepancies can be resolved mechanically versus those requiring lease or title interpretation.
fields.example: For Tract A, the system compares the approved 0.00625 decimal with every statement and flags any change. It also flags a bank mismatch above $1.00 after documented timing items. A rounding difference may close through a logged rule; an unexplained ownership change requires the land or title reviewer to approve the resolution.

fields.name: Production monitoring and decline alerts
fields.prompt: Set a monitoring baseline, reporting-lag allowance, variance threshold, and investigation sequence. Explain how revised reports, new wells, shut-ins, and lease-level aggregation affect the interpretation of apparent production changes.
fields.example: Flag a reported volume decline above 25% against the trailing three reported months, excluding periods still inside the source's normal publication lag. The reviewer checks revisions, downtime, and reporting scope before changing the forecast. If two wells share a lease-level record, the alert cannot assign the decline to one well without additional evidence.

fields.name: Pooling-docket research prioritization
fields.prompt: Specify how public docket events create research tasks and change lead priority. Record status definitions, source evidence, and safeguards against representing procedural movement as a certain near-term production catalyst.
fields.example: A filed Oklahoma pooling application creates a research task for tract coverage and owner identity. An entered order creates an election-calendar task, while a permit prompts development review. The model assigns no production revenue until supported by its explicit forecast assumptions; a protested or continued hearing reduces urgency rather than increasing price.

fields.name: Owner acquisition funnel and attribution
fields.prompt: Define the stages from researched owner through verified interest, qualified conversation, offer, diligence, and closing. Set denominator rules so conversion rates reflect unique owners and real progress rather than duplicate contacts.
fields.example: A monthly cohort contains 120 researched owners, 90 verified contact records, 18 replies, six qualified conversations, three indicative offers, and one diligence file. Reply rate is 18 divided by 90, or 20%. The diligence file is not a closed acquisition, and a second letter to the same owner does not enlarge the owner denominator.

fields.name: Outreach content and suppression workflow
fields.prompt: Write the factual message boundaries, review responsibilities, contact-frequency limits, and suppression propagation process. Explain how the team handles ownership disputes and requests to stop contact across every tool used for acquisition outreach.
fields.example: The letter says the company is interested in purchasing the described mineral interest and invites a discussion; it does not claim a mandatory sale or official affiliation. One stop-contact request updates the central suppression record before the next export. A recipient denying ownership triggers research, not a more aggressive automated follow-up.

fields.name: Manual fallback and incident owner
fields.prompt: For each critical automation, define failure detection, accountable owner, manual procedure, recovery target, and return-to-service evidence. Explain how work continues without losing accounting history or bypassing unresolved title questions.
fields.example: If the parser fails on a new operator layout, the reconciliation contractor enters the statement into the controlled review sheet within two business days. The engineer adds a fixture and validates totals before release. Automated posting resumes only after the same statement produces identical reviewed amounts and no duplicate receipt.

fields.name: Access, backups, and document protection
fields.prompt: Assign access by operating role and classify documents containing identity, bank, or tax information. Set backup, restoration, and credential-removal procedures that protect seller information while keeping authorized reviewers productive.
fields.example: The outreach contractor sees property and permitted contact records, not bank details or tax forms. Closing documents reside in a restricted repository with multifactor authentication. Revoke departing-contractor access the same day, retain access logs, and test a monthly restore using a non-sensitive ledger copy before relying on backups for production recovery.

fields.name: Automation value and escalation budget
fields.prompt: Measure saved processing time, exception volume, rework, and specialist review costs. Define when growing exception rates justify reducing automation scope instead of adding more records to an unreliable process.
fields.example: Manual reconciliation of eighty statements at fifteen minutes each takes twenty hours. Automation leaves four hours of routine work plus six hours of exception review, saving ten hours monthly. At $50 per hour, the capacity value is $500; it becomes a cash saving only if actual paid labor or outside spending declines.

worksheets.completion_gate: Deploy only after source permissions, duplicate protection, decimal alerts, suppression propagation, and manual restoration have passed documented tests; retain human review for title construction, valuation changes, disputed deductions, and owner disputes.

worksheets.title: 30-Day Launch, Pod Scorecard, and Exit-Readiness Ledger
worksheets.purpose: Launch a disciplined research and acquisition operation without mistaking a thirty-day sprint for a guaranteed closing timeline. Assign the small-team workload, track capital and quality indicators, and assemble the ownership, receipt, and basis evidence an institutional buyer needs to evaluate a mineral package.
instructions: Set the first month's deliverables around research quality, workflow testing, and qualified opportunities. Preserve the canonical six-to-twenty-four-month first-deal window, and never manufacture a closing deadline that pressures the team to bypass ownership verification or adequate capital planning.

Assign one accountable owner to each deliverable and define the contractor boundaries before outreach begins. Track the Conservative and Base staffing pattern separately from the six-person Scaled configuration so a growth plan does not silently assume unlimited support.

Use weekly reviews to compare evidence quality, cash availability, unresolved defects, and qualified lead conversion. Review volume metrics alongside rejection reasons, because a smaller clean pipeline may be more valuable than a large list with uncertain ownership.

Build the exit data room while acquiring assets rather than reconstructing it at sale. Maintain consistent tract identifiers, recorded instruments, royalty history, ownership calculations, and basis schedules that allow a buyer to reproduce the package economics independently.

End the sprint with a written continue, narrow, pause, or stop decision tied to predefined evidence. Do not equate process completion with profitable execution; continue only when capital capacity, ownership quality, and a credible acquisition thesis remain intact.

fields.name: Day 1–7 market boundary and operating setup
fields.prompt: List the first week's concrete deliverables, owners, and acceptance tests. Include the acquisition boundary, document repository, capital ledger, specialist engagement, and source inventory needed before the first owner contact.
fields.example: By day seven, the principal selects one Reeves County acquisition area, documents the $400,000 illustrative capital plan, and engages land, title, and accounting contractors. The team creates the tract ledger and tests restricted document access. Completion requires one reproducible sample ownership calculation, not a promise to acquire forty NMA immediately.

fields.name: Day 8–14 research and owner qualification
fields.prompt: Define the second week's research cohort, ownership checks, contact verification, and outreach review. State the evidence required to promote a lead from raw source record to a qualified owner opportunity.
fields.example: The land contractor researches thirty tracts and traces ten promising ownership chains. The principal reviews five complete owner packets before sending factual acquisition letters. Each packet includes the recorded reference, interest description, independently checked contact source, and suppression status. A tax-roll name alone does not qualify the lead.

fields.name: Day 15–21 underwriting and workflow rehearsal
fields.prompt: Specify the third week's valuation files, title questions, cash stresses, and technical tests. Identify the assumptions that remain conditional and the evidence needed before issuing a purchase commitment.
fields.example: Prepare three underwriting packets with verified fraction calculations, existing-production forecasts, and commodity downside cases. Rehearse the $1,562.50 gross-to-$1,425 cash statement and the duplicate-import test. The title reviewer addresses each material reservation question; the principal may issue conditional indications but cannot treat unresolved title as completed diligence.

fields.name: Day 22–30 decision and pipeline handoff
fields.prompt: Define the final week's deliverables and decision evidence. Separate offers, signed agreements, recorded acquisitions, and first royalty payments so the launch report cannot overstate commercial progress or cash realization.
fields.example: By day thirty, deliver one complete investment memorandum, an operating reconciliation demonstration, a qualified buyer profile, and the next ninety-day research plan. Report zero closed deals if none have closed. The canonical first-deal expectation remains six to twenty-four months; a successful launch establishes discipline rather than artificial revenue.

fields.name: Pod roles and specialist capacity
fields.prompt: Assign acquisition, land research, title interpretation, reconciliation, accounting, and data responsibilities within the canonical staffing envelope. Identify functions that may share one role and decisions requiring an independent specialist.
fields.example: Base uses one full-time principal plus three contractors: a land researcher, a title attorney, and a bookkeeping and tax provider. Scaled uses two full-time operators plus four contractors, adding dedicated data support. Six people is the Scaled total, not six employees plus an invisible external team excluded from the cost model.

fields.name: Weekly quality and cash scorecard
fields.prompt: Choose a compact set of quality, conversion, cash, and exception indicators with clear denominators and responsible owners. Explain which metrics signal excessive risk even when outreach activity or offers increase.
fields.example: Track verified ownership packets over researched tracts, qualified conversations over unique contacted owners, unresolved material title issues, unrestricted cash, and unmatched receipts. Ten verified packets from thirty tracts equal 33.3%. A rise to six unresolved ownership disputes pauses new commitments even if the team doubles its weekly letter volume.

fields.name: Canonical candidate and performance ledger
fields.prompt: Record the candidate's ranking, score components, capital range, monthly overhead range, and canonical profit outcomes. Keep these portfolio reference values distinct from the first month's actual activity and cash balances.
fields.example: Candidate #7, Resource assets, ranks #25 of 29 and scores 81/100: revenue potential 21, margin potential 22, team efficiency 16, startup accessibility 11, and automation potential 11. Capital is $15,000–$75,000; monthly opex is $1,000–$12,000. Canonical annual owner profits are $6,000, $69,875, and $180,000. None becomes recognized launch-month profit merely because the operating plan is complete.

fields.name: Institutional exit data-room manifest
fields.prompt: List the documents and machine-readable schedules required for buyer diligence. Assign an owner and freshness standard to each item, and explain how sensitive seller information is excluded from routine marketing materials.
fields.example: Prepare tract polygons, legal descriptions, recorded deeds, lease schedules, title memoranda, unit allocations, approved decimals, twenty-four months of available statements, and a basis bridge. Reconcile every marketed tract to the ownership ledger. Remove tax identifiers and banking details from the buyer overview, providing restricted materials only through controlled diligence access.

fields.name: Exit proceeds and owner-profit bridge
fields.prompt: Model the contemplated disposal using actual asset basis, sale proceeds, selling costs, and retained obligations. Reconcile portfolio revenue and profit without counting returned capital or unrealized marks as recognized operating income.
fields.example: The illustrative Base year receives $175,000 royalties and $160,000 Tract B proceeds. Subtract $120,000 returned basis to obtain $215,000 recognized revenue. Subtract the complete $145,125 cost schedule, including its sale-execution allocation, to obtain $69,875 profit. A higher appraisal of unsold Tract A adds nothing to this realized-revenue bridge.

fields.name: Continue, narrow, pause, or stop decision
fields.prompt: State the final operating decision, supporting evidence, capital limits, next review date, and conditions that would reverse the decision. Differentiate a temporary research pause from disposing of assets or terminating the strategy.
fields.example: Continue research within the selected county while limiting new commitments to $120,000 per fully reviewed tract. Pause purchases if unrestricted liquidity falls below the $51,000 operating-and-curative target or ownership authority remains unresolved. Review again after thirty days. A pause does not authorize a distressed sale or abandonment of existing payor reconciliation.

worksheets.completion_gate: Complete the launch only when all thirty-day deliverables are evidenced, the canonical scorecard and cash bridge reconcile, specialist responsibilities are accepted, and the next-period decision states capital limits, unresolved risks, and the documented six-to-twenty-four-month first-deal horizon.
